content: 1. Studies by Sinha (2008) and Turan, Tesfagiorghis, and Polan (2011) did not report any data on skilled birth attendance (SBA) despite interventions aimed at increasing facility-based births. 2. A program evaluation by Purdin, Khan, and Saucier (2009), using health information systems, demonstrated an increase in facility-based births among the intervention group. However, the baseline data included both refugee and non-refugee women, which may have influenced the findings. 3. In a 2004 study conducted in Indonesia, women and their husbands reported a statistically significant increase in the use of skilled birth attendants and facility-based births among the exposed group. 4. A 2004 study in Nepal revealed that women in the unexposed group reported an increase in the presence of skilled birth attendants (doctors) and facility-based births. However, this finding was contradicted by their husbands, who reported an increase in SBA and facility-based births for the exposed group. 5. Care involving a skilled birth attendant or facility was emphasized in cases of maternal complications or illness. However, there was a potential for selection bias, as allocation concealment was unlikely, and outcome assessors were likely aware of participants' intervention status. Women were also unlikely to be blinded to cluster allocation (Midhet and Becker, 2010). 6. The study populations were poorly described, with limited details beyond women residing in predetermined villages or clusters. These studies were conducted in low-income rural settings. 7. Multifaceted interventions included providing women with information on safe motherhood through pictorial booklets and audio cassettes, training traditional birth attendants in clean delivery practices and recognition of obstetric and newborn complications, and establishing emergency transportation systems. In eight of the 16 intervention clusters, husbands also received educational materials on safe motherhood and family planning. 8. Trials compared interventions with either control groups or interventions without male involvement. However, there was a lack of clarity on methods, unreliable data collection, and insufficient information about participant recruitment and selection. 9. In one study, women attending antenatal care (ANC) services at Employee State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) clinics during 10–26 weeks of gestation were included. Both husband and wife were expected to reside at the same address six months postpartum. The study assessed the impact of male involvement interventions on postpartum family planning and STI prevention practices. 10. Another study included married women attending ANC with their husbands, excluding those living more than 90 minutes away from the facility. Conducted in a low-income urban setting, the intervention consisted of two 35-minute educational sessions delivered in private hospital rooms. 11. Data on ANC visits showed no significant differences between study groups in attending more than three ANC visits. However, one quasi-experimental study reported a statistically significant increase in more than one and more than four ANC visits. 12. Breastfeeding interventions showed potential selection bias, as it was unclear how clusters were initially randomized. The study populations were poorly described, and interventions were conducted in low-income settings. 13. Male involvement interventions varied widely. For example, one study used a single educational program for expectant fathers, covering topics such as health and nutrition during pregnancy, ANC, childbirth support, breastfeeding, postpartum care, contraception, communication techniques, and adjustment to fatherhood. 14. In another study, male involvement was part of a larger program based on the Safe Motherhood Initiative, making it difficult to isolate the male involvement component. 15. A program evaluation study showed an increase in postnatal care within 72 hours of birth following the intervention. 16. A cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) of moderate quality reported a significant increase in facility-based births through a community scorecard process. This intervention informed the community about their rights to access quality care, developed action plans, and monitored health facility accountability. 17. Observational studies of weak methodological quality addressed safe motherhood at community, family, and individual levels. Youth and local representatives raised awareness about rights and supported review meetings to improve services. Monthly meetings fostered family support and engagement. 18. Overall, the quality of evidence varied, with some studies showing serious risks of bias, indirectness, and inconsistency. The effectiveness of interventions promoting awareness of human rights, sexual and reproductive rights, and access to skilled care remains challenging to assess due to methodological limitations.
